qs.q: An orthopedic surgeon repairs a torn Achilles tendon. Which dense investing membrane must be incised or reflected to fully expose the paratenon and deep tendon fibers in the lower leg?
o: The interosseous membrane of the lower leg
The deep crural fascia of the posterior calf
qs.e: The deep crural fascia invests the calf muscles and covers the Achilles tendon before blending near the calcaneus.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Aponeurosis - Anatomy Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 30-year-old male sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture following a motorcycle crash. Eight hours later, he develops severe, disproportionate pain in his lower leg that worsens with passive toe extension, alongside tense, wooden compartments. What is the fundamental pathophysiology causing muscle and nerve necrosis in this condition?
o: Bacterial superinfection of the deep fascial planes
Primary arterial laceration leading to immediate distal gangrene
Direct thermal injury to the epimysium from the fracture hematoma
Elevated intracompartmental pressure causing venous obstruction and capillary collapse
qs.e: Acute compartment syndrome occurs when a rise in pressure within a closed osteofascial compartment exceeds venous pressure, leading to venous obstruction, capillary collapse, and subsequent ischaemia. Arterial laceration causes different ischemic syndromes rather than isolated intercompartmental pressure elevation.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after being bitten by a venomous snake on his lower leg. Within hours, he experiences massive leg swelling, severe pain out of proportion, and loss of two-point discrimination in the foot. What specific diagnosis must the surgical team immediately evaluate for?
qs.e: Snake bites are explicitly listed as a cause of increased contents leading to acute compartment syndrome, characterized by severe pain and neurological deficits. While necrotizing fasciitis can follow bites, the acute tense swelling points directly to compartment syndrome.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with a spreading red, hot, swollen, tender lesion on his lower leg with ill-defined borders and red streaks tracking to the groin. What is the commonest causative organism?
qs.e: Cellulitis is most commonly caused by beta-haemolytic streptococci (groups A, B, C, G), followed by Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas and Escherichia coli are uncommon primary pathogens for typical community-acquired non-suppurative lower limb cellulitis.
qs.s: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections, and Snake Bites: MCQs

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman develops tense swelling of her lower leg following a puff adder bite. Her diastolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg and measured compartment pressure is 55 mmHg. She also has active venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. What is the most appropriate surgical timing and management regarding fasciotomy?
o: Delay any surgical intervention for 48 hours until all systemic antivenom effects wear off completely.
Correct the coagulation abnormalities first, then perform fasciotomy if compartment pressure remains elevated.
Perform an immediate emergency fasciotomy regardless of the coagulation status to prevent ischaemia.
Perform needle aspiration of the fascial compartments instead of an open surgical release.
qs.e: Fasciotomy should not be done in snake-bite coagulopathy before correcting the clotting due to bleeding risk, and is considered when compartment pressure exceeds 40 mmHg after correction. Immediate fasciotomy without correcting coagulation leads to severe hemorrhage.
qs.s: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections, and Snake Bites: MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old male with chronic varicose veins presents with brown pigmentation and induration with fibrosis giving an 'inverted champagne bottle' appearance of his lower leg. What is the most accurate term for this specific cutaneous manifestation?
qs.e: Lipodermatosclerosis is induration with fibrosis leading to an 'inverted champagne bottle' leg. Haemosiderin pigmentation is the brown discoloration often seen as an early sign near the ankle.
qs.s: Varicose Veins and Chronic Venous Insufficiency of the Leg: MCQs

qs.q: A 54-year-old diabetic man presents with a rapidly spreading erythematous lesion on his right lower leg following a minor scratch. He is tachycardic and febrile, but physical examination reveals only mild overlying erythema and swelling, yet he complains of excruciating pain that makes him weep. What is the most appropriate initial conclusion regarding this presentation?
o: The presentation is typical of simple localized subcutaneous abscess formation.
The clinical severity points strongly toward necrotising fasciitis due to pain out of proportion.
The systemic signs indicate primary clostridial myonecrosis without fascial involvement.
The mild findings rule out necrotising fasciitis, confirming uncomplicated cellulitis.
qs.e: Severe pain out of proportion to physical findings is the key early pointer to necrotising fasciitis, which often resembles simple cellulitis initially. Uncomplicated cellulitis would not present with such severe pain or profound systemic illness relative to the minor physical appearance.
qs.s: Necrotising Fasciitis and Fournier's Gangrene: MCQs

qs.q: A 51-year-old woman has 5 months of progressive lower leg swelling. CXR shows bilateral pleural effusions and prominent right heart border. AST, ALT, and LDH are elevated; CK is normal. Most likely underlying disease?
qs.e: Recurrent pulmonary emboli → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure → hepatic passive congestion → elevated transaminases and LDH but normal CK (no myocardial ischemia).

ai.title: Lower Leg Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The lower leg contains the tibia, fibula, and a complex network of muscles, nerves and vessels. Clinically, its anatomy guides the diagnosis of fractures, vascular disease, infections and pressure ulcers common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The lower leg is the segment between the knee and the ankle, comprising bone, muscle, nerve and vascular structures that support ambulation and maintain venous return.
b: Tibia and fibula form the skeleton
Muscle compartments: anterior, lateral, deep posterior, superficial posterior
Saphenous nerve supplies sensation to medial leg

sections.p: The tibia is the weight‑bearing bone; the fibula is thinner and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments.
The lower leg lies posterior to the thigh and anterior to the foot. Key relations include the popliteal fossa behind, the tibial nerve and artery medially, and the peroneal nerve laterally.
b: Saphenous vein runs with saphenous nerve
Peroneal nerve wraps around fibular head

sections.p: The popliteal artery bifurcates into the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal arteries, supplying the compartments.

t.b: Assesses anterior tibial artery patency; loss of dorsiflexion suggests arterial insufficiency.

sections.p: Sensory: saphenous nerve (medial leg), superficial peroneal nerve (lateral leg). Motor: deep peroneal (extensors), tibial nerve (flexors).
b: Loss of sensation over medial malleolus = saphenous neuropathy
Foot drop = deep peroneal nerve injury

sections.p: Supports weight, facilitates gait, and protects the ankle joint. Muscle compartments allow flexion, extension, inversion and eversion.
Fractures, compartment syndrome, venous stasis, infections (tetanus, cellulitis), pressure ulcers and peripheral arterial disease are common.
b: Low‑resource settings see malaria‑related anemia leading to leg swelling

t.b: Detects peripheral arterial disease; absent pulse indicates severe occlusion.
Screen for chronic venous insufficiency; >34 cm suggests significant edema.
Elevated in cellulitis; normal in early venous stasis.

sections.p: Use a systematic approach: history of trauma, vascular risk factors, infection signs, and ulcer characteristics. Check pulses, capillary refill, skin temperature and color.
b: Ask about recent falls or infections
Palpate for tenderness and compartment pressure if suspected

sections.p: Differential includes deep vein thrombosis, cellulitis, venous stasis, and pressure ulcer.
b: DVT: pain, swelling, calf tenderness, positive Homan sign

sections.p: In malaria endemic areas, anemia can mask hypovolemia; low-grade fever may be missed in chronic infections.
b: Normal WCC can occur in early cellulitis

sections.p: Treat underlying cause: antibiotics for infection, anticoagulation for DVT, surgical decompression for compartment syndrome. Supportive care includes elevation, compression stockings and wound care.
Urgent referral if sudden severe pain, swelling, loss of pulses, or signs of systemic infection.
b: Pain out of proportion to injury

faq.a: Increased pressure within a muscle compartment that compromises circulation and nerve function.

faq.q: How do you differentiate venous stasis from cellulitis?
faq.a: Venous stasis: chronic, painless swelling, skin changes; cellulitis: acute pain, warmth, erythema, fever.

faq.q: Why is the saphenous nerve important?
faq.a: It provides sensation to the medial leg; injury can cause numbness and affect wound care.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man presents with a swollen, painful left calf after a fall. What is the next best step? — Check pulses, perform a Doppler, and if pulses are absent, arrange urgent vascular imaging.
A 50‑year‑old diabetic woman has a non‑healing ulcer above the medial malleolus. What is the first investigation? — X‑ray to rule out osteomyelitis; if negative, start wound care and compression.

A 28‑year‑old woman with sudden calf pain and swelling after a long flight. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Deep vein thrombosis; give low‑molecular‑weight heparin and refer for ultrasound.
A 60‑year‑old man with chronic leg swelling and shiny skin. What is the most likely cause? — Chronic venous insufficiency; assess ankle‑brachial index and start compression therapy.
A 45‑year‑old man with a tibial fracture and increasing pain out of proportion to injury. What is the emergency treatment? — Suspect compartment syndrome; perform immediate fasciotomy.
A 70‑year‑old woman with a painless ulcer on the foot. What is the differential? — Peripheral arterial disease, neuropathy, and pressure ulcer; assess pulses and sensory testing.
